title: Real-Time Data Streaming with Apache Kafka
subtitle: Run Kafka 4 in KRaft mode, write reliable Python producers and consumers, use transactions and schemas, and build windowed stream processing that copes with late data.
outcomes: Run Kafka 4 in KRaft mode and design topics, keys and partitions for the ordering and parallelism you need
Write Python producers and consumer groups that deliver at least once, with idempotent producers and deliberate offset commits
Build exactly-once consume-transform-produce pipelines with transactions, and explain what they don't cover
Evolve Avro schemas safely using backward, forward and full compatibility and the registry wire format
Process streams with tables, event-time windows, grace periods and joins, and keep their state fault-tolerant
prerequisites: Confident Python and the command line (Linux Command Line Essentials), and the batch and streaming basics of Data Engineering Foundations: Batch and Streaming Pipelines. Docker basics from Containerisation and Orchestration with Docker and Kubernetes help. Install Python 3.10 or later and Docker, or Java 17 or later for the Kafka download. Enterprise Data and ML Platforms covers streaming architecture across a whole organisation.
description:
Apache Kafka is where many organisations keep their events: orders, payments, sensor readings and clicks, stored as durable logs that many applications read independently. This course teaches how Kafka works and how to build on it correctly. You'll run Kafka 4, which needs no ZooKeeper, in KRaft mode on your laptop, see how keys choose partitions and what that means for ordering, and write Python producers and consumers with confluent-kafka that report every delivery and commit offsets on purpose. Then you'll make pipelines reliable with replication, idempotent producers and transactions, and find out exactly where exactly-once stops.

The second half covers what keeps streaming systems running for years: schemas that evolve without breaking consumers, with the registry wire format and Avro's compatibility rules, and stream processing with tables, event-time windows, grace periods, joins and fault-tolerant state. Every module has a lab against a real broker, with starter code whose output is the same on every run: you'll crash consumers on purpose to see at-most-once and at-least-once, abort a transaction and read around it, and build a windowed processor that drops late events. The capstone is a real-time delivery monitor that survives crashes and schema changes.

modules.title: Kafka's model: logs, topics, partitions and offsets
modules.summary: What an event log is and how Kafka stores one: brokers, topics, partitions, offsets, retention and compaction, how keys decide partitions and ordering, and how to run Kafka 4 in KRaft mode on a laptop.

lessons.title: Event streaming and the log
objectives: Describe Kafka's log-based model of records, topics and offsets
Explain how retention and compaction decide what a topic keeps
key_points: Kafka stores streams of records in topics; a record has a key, a value, a timestamp and optional headers, and once written it is never changed, only appended to and eventually removed.
Each topic is split into partitions, and each partition is an ordered, append-only log on a broker's disk in which every record has a sequential offset: 0, 1, 2 and so on.
Unlike a traditional message queue, reading doesn't delete anything: each consumer tracks its own offset, so many independent applications can read the same topic, and can rewind to reprocess it.
Retention decides how long records are kept, by time (retention.ms, 7 days by default) or by size per partition (retention.bytes); old log segments are deleted whether or not anyone has read them.

A compacted topic (cleanup.policy=compact) keeps at least the latest record for each key, which suits changelogs such as a customer's current address; a record with a null value, a tombstone, deletes its key.

lessons.title: Partitions, keys and ordering
objectives: Predict which partition a keyed record goes to
Choose keys and partition counts that keep the ordering you need
key_points: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, so records that must stay in order, such as every event for one delivery rider, must share a key and therefore a partition.
Java clients send a keyed record to murmur2(key) modulo the number of partitions; records without a key are spread across partitions by a sticky partitioner that fills one batch at a time.
librdkafka-based clients, including Python's confluent-kafka, default to a different hash (consistent_random); set partitioner=murmur2_random so they place keys exactly where Java clients do.
Partitions are the unit of parallelism: a consumer group can have at most one active consumer per partition, so the partition count caps how far consumption can scale out.

Adding partitions later changes which partition a key maps to, which breaks per-key ordering across the change, so choose the count up front; with few keys, hashing can also leave partitions hot or empty.

lessons.title: Running Kafka in KRaft mode
objectives: Explain what KRaft replaced and how a Kafka 4 cluster is organised
Start a single-node broker with Docker or the Apache download
key_points: Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper: a cluster's metadata (topics, partitions, configuration and leaders) now lives in an internal Raft-replicated log managed by controller nodes, known as KRaft mode, which has been production-ready since Kafka 3.3.
Each node has process.roles of broker, controller or both; production clusters run separate controllers, usually three, while a laptop runs one combined node.

Before its first start, a KRaft node's storage is formatted with a cluster ID: kafka-storage.sh random-uuid makes one and kafka-storage.sh format writes it, with --standalone for a single-controller set-up.

Listeners say where the node accepts connections and advertised.listeners what it tells clients to connect to; a wrong advertised address is the usual reason a client can reach the bootstrap server but then times out.
The Apache Kafka project publishes an official Docker image, apache/kafka, whose default configuration runs a single combined node on localhost:9092, with the command-line tools in /opt/kafka/bin.

files.content:
"""Predict the partition Kafka's Java clients choose for a key: murmur2(key) & 0x7fffffff % partitions.

Usage:  python which_partition.py 3 rider-07 rider-12 rider-31 rider-44

The console producer and other Java clients use this default partitioner for keyed records.
confluent-kafka (librdkafka) uses a different default; set partitioner=murmur2_random to match.
"""
import sys

MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF


def murmur2(data: bytes) -> int:
    """Kafka's 32-bit murmur2 hash (org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils.murmur2)."""
    m, r = 0x5BD1E995, 24
    h = (0x9747B28C ^ len(data)) & MASK
    whole = len(data) // 4
    for i in range(whole):
        k = int.from_bytes(data[i * 4:i * 4 + 4], "little")
        k = (k * m) & MASK
        k ^= k >> r
        k = (k * m) & MASK
        h = (h * m) & MASK
        h ^= k
    tail = data[whole * 4:]
    if len(tail) >= 3:
        h ^= tail[2] << 16
    if len(tail) >= 2:
        h ^= tail[1] << 8
    if len(tail) >= 1:
        h ^= tail[0]
        h = (h * m) & MASK
    h ^= h >> 13
    h = (h * m) & MASK
    h ^= h >> 15
    return h


def partition_for(key: str, partitions: int) -> int:
    return (murmur2(key.encode("utf-8")) & 0x7FFFFFFF) % partitions


if __name__ == "__main__":
    count = int(sys.argv[1])
    for key in sys.argv[2:]:
        print(f"{key} -> partition {partition_for(key, count)}")

modules.title: Producers and consumers in Python
modules.summary: How a producer batches, acknowledges and reports on what it sends, how consumer groups share partitions and rebalance, and how the moment you commit an offset decides between at-most-once and at-least-once delivery.

lessons.title: How a producer sends: batching, acks and delivery reports
objectives: Explain how a producer batches and acknowledges records
Use delivery reports to know what was really written
key_points: produce() only queues a record in the client's memory; a background thread groups records for the same partition into batches and sends them, so a record isn't safe until the broker acknowledges it.

linger.ms makes the producer wait a few milliseconds to fill bigger batches and batch.size caps a batch's bytes; compression.type, such as lz4 or zstd, compresses whole batches, which saves network and disk.
acks=0 doesn't wait at all, acks=1 waits for the partition leader to write the record, and acks=all waits until every in-sync replica has it, the setting to use when losing data matters.

In confluent-kafka, a delivery callback passed to produce() runs once per record, from poll() or flush(), with an error or the record's partition and offset; call poll(0) regularly and flush() before exiting, or queued records are lost.
Retries handle temporary errors such as a leader moving; without idempotence, a retry after a lost acknowledgement can write a record twice or out of order, which the next module fixes.

lessons.title: Consumer groups, assignment and rebalancing
objectives: Explain how a consumer group divides partitions among its members
Describe what triggers a rebalance and how to make rebalances less disruptive
key_points: Consumers sharing a group.id form a consumer group: each partition is read by exactly one member at a time, so adding consumers spreads the work, up to one consumer per partition; extra members sit idle.

A broker acts as the group coordinator; members send heartbeats, and one that stops for session.timeout.ms, or doesn't call poll() within max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes by default), is removed and its partitions are reassigned.

A rebalance happens when members join or leave or the subscribed topics change; with the classic eager protocol every member stops consuming during it, while cooperative assignment (cooperative-sticky) moves only the partitions that must move.
Kafka 4 also offers a newer consumer group protocol, enabled with group.protocol=consumer, in which the broker works out assignments incrementally; the classic protocol is still the clients' default.
Static membership, a fixed group.instance.id per consumer, lets a restarted consumer take back its partitions within the session timeout without triggering a rebalance.
Consumer lag is the log-end offset minus the group's committed offset for each partition; kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe shows it, and lag that keeps growing means consumers can't keep up.

lessons.title: Offsets, commits and delivery semantics
objectives: Distinguish at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery
Commit offsets at the right moment for the guarantee you need
key_points: A committed offset is the position a group will resume from: the offset of the next record to read, one more than the last record processed, stored in Kafka's internal __consumer_offsets topic.

With enable.auto.commit, the default, offsets are committed in the background every few seconds, so a crash can repeat records processed since the last commit or skip records polled but not yet processed.
Committing before processing gives at-most-once: a crash after the commit loses the record. Processing before committing gives at-least-once: a crash before the commit processes the record again.
At-least-once is the usual choice, paired with idempotent processing, such as upserts keyed on an event ID or ignoring IDs already seen, so a repeat changes nothing.

auto.offset.reset decides where a group with no committed offset starts: latest (the default) reads only new records, earliest reads the whole retained log; kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets rewinds an inactive group to reprocess.

files.content:
"""The lab's delivery events: 15 orders, each picked up and then delivered, by six riders in five zones."""

RIDERS = ["rider-01", "rider-02", "rider-03", "rider-04", "rider-05", "rider-06"]
ZONES = ["Silom", "Ari", "Thonglor", "Bang Rak", "Sathorn"]


def delivery_events():
    events = []
    for n in range(15):
        order = {"order_id": 6001 + n, "rider": RIDERS[n % 6], "zone": ZONES[(n * 2) % 5],
                 "amount": round(80 + (n * 37) % 120 + 0.5 * (n % 2), 2)}
        events.append({**order, "event": "picked_up"})
        events.append({**order, "event": "delivered"})
    return events

"""Send the delivery events to the rider-events topic, keyed by rider, and report where they landed.

Usage:  python producer.py
"""
import json
from collections import Counter

from confluent_kafka import Producer

from events import delivery_events

TOPIC = "rider-events"

config = {
    "bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092",
    "acks": "all",                       # wait for every in-sync replica
    "enable.idempotence": True,          # no duplicates or reordering from retries
    "linger.ms": 20,                     # wait up to 20 ms to fill a batch
    "compression.type": "lz4",           # compress whole batches
    "partitioner": "murmur2_random",     # the same key-to-partition mapping as Java clients
}

delivered = Counter()
failed = []


def on_delivery(err, msg):
    """Called once per message from poll() or flush(), when the broker has acknowledged it (or given up)."""
    if err is not None:
        failed.append(err)
    else:
        delivered[msg.partition()] += 1


def main():
    producer = Producer(config)
    for event in delivery_events():
        producer.produce(TOPIC, key=event["rider"], value=json.dumps(event), on_delivery=on_delivery)
        producer.poll(0)                 # serve delivery callbacks that are ready
    remaining = producer.flush(10)       # wait for every outstanding message
    print(f"Delivered {sum(delivered.values())} events, {len(failed)} failed, {remaining} still queued")
    for partition, count in sorted(delivered.items()):
        print(f"  partition {partition}: {count} events")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Read rider events in a consumer group, committing offsets by hand.

Usage:
    python consumer.py --group audit                   # read until the topic is quiet for 5 seconds
    python consumer.py --group amo --crash-after 12    # die while handling the 12th event
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
from collections import Counter

from confluent_kafka import Consumer, KafkaException

TOPIC = "rider-events"
assigned = []


def on_assign(consumer, partitions):
    assigned[:] = sorted(p.partition for p in partitions)
    print("Assigned partitions:", assigned)


def handle(msg, delivered_by_zone):
    """Process one event: here, count deliveries by zone."""
    event = json.loads(msg.value())
    if event["event"] == "delivered":
        delivered_by_zone[event["zone"]] += 1
    print(f"p{msg.partition()} offset {msg.offset()}: order {event['order_id']} {event['event']}")


def crash_point(seen, crash_after, processed):
    if seen == crash_after:
        print(f"Simulated crash while handling event {seen}: {processed} events processed")
        os._exit(1)                        # no commit, no clean shutdown


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--group", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--crash-after", type=int, default=0)
    parser.add_argument("--idle-seconds", type=int, default=5)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    consumer = Consumer({
        "bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092",
        "group.id": args.group,
        "auto.offset.reset": "earliest",   # a new group starts from the oldest message
        "enable.auto.commit": False,       # commit by hand
        "session.timeout.ms": 10000,       # a crashed member is noticed after 10 seconds
    })
    consumer.subscribe([TOPIC], on_assign=on_assign)
    seen, processed, idle = 0, 0, 0
    delivered_by_zone = Counter()
    try:
        while idle < args.idle_seconds:
            msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
            if msg is None:
                idle += 1 if assigned else 0   # don't count the wait for an assignment
                continue
            if msg.error():
                raise KafkaException(msg.error())
            idle = 0
            seen += 1
            # TODO: this commits the offset before the event is processed, which is at-most-once.
            # Swap the order so the event is processed first and then committed (at-least-once).
            consumer.commit(message=msg, asynchronous=False)
            crash_point(seen, args.crash_after, processed)
            handle(msg, delivered_by_zone)
            processed += 1
    finally:
        consumer.close()
    print(f"Processed {processed} events; deliveries by zone: {dict(sorted(delivered_by_zone.items()))}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: A group remembers its offsets, so each experiment uses a new group name; reusing one starts where it left off.
If the restarted consumer prints nothing for a while, it's waiting for the crashed member's session to time out: that's the point of the experiment.
In the at-least-once order, crash_point() goes after handle() and before commit().
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe works whether or not the group's consumers are running.

modules.title: Reliability: replication, idempotence and transactions
modules.summary: How Kafka keeps data when brokers fail, how idempotent producers stop retries from duplicating records, and how transactions give exactly-once consume-transform-produce, along with what they can't promise.

lessons.title: Replication, in-sync replicas and durability
objectives: Explain how leaders, followers and in-sync replicas protect data
Choose replication and acknowledgement settings for durability
key_points: Each partition has replication.factor copies on different brokers: one leader that handles writes and, by default, reads, and followers that copy from it; three replicas is the usual production choice.

The in-sync replicas (ISR) are the replicas caught up with the leader; consumers only see records up to the high watermark, the offset every in-sync replica has, so they never read a record that could vanish in a failover.

With acks=all a write succeeds once every in-sync replica has it, and min.insync.replicas, commonly 2 with three replicas, makes such writes fail with NotEnoughReplicas when too few replicas are in sync.

If a leader fails, a controller elects a new leader from the in-sync replicas; unclean.leader.election.enable, false by default, would let an out-of-date replica lead and lose records in exchange for availability.
Spreading replicas across racks or availability zones with broker.rack means one rack or zone can fail without losing a partition; a topic can't have more replicas than the cluster has brokers.

lessons.title: Idempotent producers
objectives: Explain how an idempotent producer prevents duplicates and reordering from retries
Know where idempotence stops and application-level duplicates begin
key_points: An idempotent producer gets a producer ID from the cluster and numbers each record it sends to a partition; the broker rejects a sequence number it has already written, so a retried batch is stored once.
It also keeps order across retries with up to five in-flight requests per connection, so throughput doesn't suffer for it.
Java producers enable idempotence by default since Kafka 3.0, together with acks=all; in librdkafka clients such as confluent-kafka, set enable.idempotence=true, which also sets acks=all.

Idempotence covers retries within one producer session and partition: if the application restarts and sends the same event again, it gets a new producer ID and the broker can't tell, so events still need their own IDs for downstream deduplication.

lessons.title: Transactions and exactly-once processing
objectives: Describe how Kafka transactions make consume-transform-produce exactly once
Explain the limits of exactly-once, and what consumers must set
key_points: A transactional producer has a transactional.id that stays the same across restarts; init_transactions() registers it with a transaction coordinator and fences any older instance with the same ID, so a zombie can't commit.

Between begin_transaction() and commit_transaction(), records to any number of partitions, plus the consumer's offsets added with send_offsets_to_transaction(), succeed or fail together; abort_transaction() discards them all.

Aborted records stay in the log, followed by an abort marker; consumers with isolation.level=read_committed skip them and read only up to the last stable offset, while read_uncommitted, the Java client's default, sees everything.
Commit and abort markers take up offsets too, so a transactional topic's offsets have gaps, and its end offset is higher than its record count.

Exactly-once covers reading from and writing to Kafka: a side effect outside it, such as a database write, an email or an HTTP call, can still happen twice, so make it idempotent or write it through an outbox or a connector that supports exactly-once.
Kafka Streams turns all of this on with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2; transactions add latency and coordinator traffic, so use them where duplicates actually cost something.

"""Send 12 payments to the payments topic with an idempotent producer.

Usage:  python send_payments.py
"""
import json

from confluent_kafka import Producer

PAYMENTS = [  # payment_id, order_id, amount, currency
    (1, 7001, 450.00, "THB"), (2, 7002, 120.50, "THB"), (3, 7003, -20.00, "THB"), (4, 7004, 300.00, "USD"),
    (5, 7005, 99.00, "THB"), (6, 7006, 0.00, "THB"), (7, 7007, 250.00, "THB"), (8, 7008, 75.25, "THB"),
    (9, 7009, 610.00, "THB"), (10, 7010, 45.00, "EUR"), (11, 7011, 180.00, "THB"), (12, 7012, 32.75, "THB"),
]


def main():
    producer = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092", "enable.idempotence": True})
    for payment_id, order_id, amount, currency in PAYMENTS:
        value = {"payment_id": payment_id, "order_id": order_id, "amount": amount, "currency": currency}
        producer.produce("payments", key=str(order_id), value=json.dumps(value))
    producer.flush(10)
    print(f"Sent {len(PAYMENTS)} payments")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Validate payments exactly once: read payments, write each to payments-valid or payments-rejected,
and commit the input offsets in the same transaction as the output.

Usage:
    python validator.py                 # process everything, in batches of 4
    python validator.py --fail-batch 2  # abort the second batch's transaction, then stop
"""
import argparse
import json

from confluent_kafka import Consumer, KafkaException, Producer

BATCH = 4


def check(payment):
    """Return the reason a payment is rejected, or None if it's valid."""
    if payment["amount"] <= 0:
        return "amount must be positive"
    if payment["currency"] != "THB":
        return "currency must be THB"
    return None


def next_batch(consumer, size, idle_seconds=5):
    batch, idle = [], 0
    while len(batch) < size and idle < idle_seconds:
        msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
        if msg is None:
            idle += 1
            continue
        if msg.error():
            raise KafkaException(msg.error())
        batch.append(msg)
    return batch


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--fail-batch", type=int, default=0)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    producer = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092",
                         "transactional.id": "payment-validator"})   # stable across restarts
    producer.init_transactions()       # registers the id and fences any older instance using it
    consumer = Consumer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092",
                         "group.id": "payment-validator",
                         "auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
                         "enable.auto.commit": False,               # offsets go into the transaction
                         "isolation.level": "read_committed"})
    consumer.subscribe(["payments"])
    number = 0
    try:
        while batch := next_batch(consumer, BATCH):
            number += 1
            producer.begin_transaction()
            for msg in batch:
                payment = json.loads(msg.value())
                reason = check(payment)
                if reason:
                    producer.produce("payments-rejected", key=msg.key(), value=json.dumps({**payment, "reason": reason}))
                else:
                    producer.produce("payments-valid", key=msg.key(), value=msg.value())
            if number == args.fail_batch:
                producer.flush()               # the batch's output reaches the log...
                producer.abort_transaction()   # ...and is then marked as aborted
                print(f"Batch {number}: aborted after writing {len(batch)} results; stopping")
                return
            # TODO: add the consumer's current positions to this transaction (send_offsets_to_transaction
            # takes the positions of the assigned partitions and the consumer's group metadata), then
            # commit the transaction, so the results and the input offsets commit together or not at all.
            print(f"Batch {number}: committed {len(batch)} payments, input offsets up to {batch[-1].offset()}")
    finally:
        consumer.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Print every record in a topic as a consumer with the given isolation level sees it.

Usage:  python read_topic.py payments-valid read_committed
        python read_topic.py payments-valid read_uncommitted
"""
import sys
import uuid

from confluent_kafka import OFFSET_BEGINNING, Consumer, TopicPartition


def main():
    topic, level = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    consumer = Consumer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092", "group.id": f"reader-{uuid.uuid4()}",
                         "isolation.level": level, "enable.auto.commit": False})
    partitions = consumer.list_topics(topic, timeout=10).topics[topic].partitions
    consumer.assign([TopicPartition(topic, p, OFFSET_BEGINNING) for p in sorted(partitions)])
    records, idle = [], 0
    while idle < 3:
        msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
        if msg is None:
            idle += 1
            continue
        if not msg.error():
            records.append(msg.value().decode())
    consumer.close()
    print(f"{topic} ({level}): {len(records)} records")
    for value in records:
        print("  ", value)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Schemas and evolution on the wire
modules.summary: Why streams need schemas, how a schema registry and its wire format work, and which schema changes are backward, forward or fully compatible, checked by actually reading old data with new schemas and new data with old ones.

lessons.title: Serialisation formats and the schema registry
objectives: Compare JSON, Avro and Protobuf for Kafka records
Explain how a schema registry and its wire format connect producers and consumers
key_points: Kafka stores keys and values as bytes and never checks them, so producers and consumers must agree on a format; a schema makes that agreement explicit and testable.

JSON is readable but repeats field names in every record and has no enforced types; Avro and Protobuf are compact binary formats whose readers need the schema, and both are designed for schemas that evolve.

A schema registry, such as Confluent Schema Registry, Apicurio Registry or Karapace, stores versions of each subject's schema, gives each schema an ID, and rejects new versions that break the subject's compatibility rule.
By default a subject is named after the topic, such as payments-value for the values in payments, so every record in a topic is checked against one evolving schema.
Registry serialisers write a magic byte of 0, then the schema ID as a 4-byte big-endian integer, then the encoded record; a consumer reads the ID, fetches and caches that writer schema, and decodes.

Avro decoding resolves the writer's schema against the reader's: fields the reader doesn't know are skipped, fields missing from the data take the reader's default, and some types can be promoted, such as int to long.

lessons.title: Compatibility rules and safe changes
objectives: Classify schema changes as backward, forward or fully compatible
Plan the order in which producers and consumers upgrade
key_points: BACKWARD compatibility, Confluent Schema Registry's default, means the new schema can read data written with the previous one, so consumers upgrade first; FORWARD means the previous schema can read new data, so producers upgrade first.
FULL means both directions work, so either side can upgrade first; the _TRANSITIVE variants check against every earlier version, not just the latest, which matters when a topic keeps old data.

Adding a field with a default, or a nullable field defaulting to null, is fully compatible; adding a field without a default breaks backward compatibility, because the new reader has nothing to fill it with in old data.

Deleting a field breaks forward compatibility unless the field had a default, because old readers still expect it; renaming is a delete plus an add, though an Avro alias lets the new reader find the old name.

Changing a type is usually breaking, except promotions such as int to long, which old data survives but old readers can't read; when a change must break, publish to a new topic or subject and migrate consumers.
In Protobuf, every field has a number: never reuse or change a field's number, and mark removed numbers as reserved so nobody reuses them later.

"""Avro helpers for the lab: the schemas, a stand-in for a schema registry, and the Confluent wire format.

The wire format a schema registry's serialisers use is: one magic byte (0), the schema's ID as a
4-byte big-endian integer, then the Avro binary encoding of the record.
"""
import io
import json
import struct
from pathlib import Path

import fastavro

SCHEMAS = json.loads((Path(__file__).parent / "schemas.json").read_text())
REGISTRY = {1: "v1", 2: "v2"}     # schema ID -> version, as a registry would assign them


def parsed(version):
    return fastavro.parse_schema(SCHEMAS[version])


def encode(record, schema_id):
    out = io.BytesIO()
    out.write(struct.pack(">bI", 0, schema_id))
    fastavro.schemaless_writer(out, parsed(REGISTRY[schema_id]), record)
    return out.getvalue()


def decode(data, reader_version):
    """Find the writer's schema from the ID in the message, then resolve it to the reader's schema."""
    magic, schema_id = struct.unpack(">bI", data[:5])
    if magic != 0:
        raise ValueError("not in the registry wire format")
    writer = parsed(REGISTRY[schema_id])
    record = fastavro.schemaless_reader(io.BytesIO(data[5:]), writer, parsed(reader_version))
    return schema_id, record


def can_read(writer_version, reader_version, record):
    """Write a record with one schema and read it with another; return (ok, error message)."""
    out = io.BytesIO()
    fastavro.schemaless_writer(out, parsed(writer_version), record)
    out.seek(0)
    try:
        fastavro.schemaless_reader(out, parsed(writer_version), parsed(reader_version))
        return True, ""
    except Exception as exc:  # fastavro raises SchemaResolutionError and friends
        return False, str(exc).splitlines()[0]

"""Send Avro payments in the registry wire format: three written with schema 1 (v1), two with schema 2 (v2).

Usage:  python avro_produce.py
"""
from confluent_kafka import Producer

from avro_tools import encode

OLD = [{"payment_id": n, "order_id": 7000 + n, "amount": 100.0 * n, "currency": "THB"} for n in (1, 2, 3)]
NEW = [{"payment_id": n, "order_id": 7000 + n, "amount": 100.0 * n, "currency": "THB", "channel": "kiosk"}
       for n in (4, 5)]


def main():
    producer = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092", "enable.idempotence": True})
    for record in OLD:
        producer.produce("payments-avro", key=str(record["order_id"]), value=encode(record, 1))
    for record in NEW:
        producer.produce("payments-avro", key=str(record["order_id"]), value=encode(record, 2))
    producer.flush(10)
    print(f"Sent {len(OLD)} records with schema ID 1 and {len(NEW)} with schema ID 2")
    print("First bytes of a schema 2 message:", encode(NEW[0], 2)[:5].hex(" "))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Read the Avro payments as a consumer whose code was built against one schema version.

Usage:  python avro_consume.py v1
        python avro_consume.py v2
"""
import sys
import uuid

from confluent_kafka import OFFSET_BEGINNING, Consumer, TopicPartition

from avro_tools import decode


def main():
    reader = sys.argv[1]
    consumer = Consumer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092", "group.id": f"avro-{uuid.uuid4()}",
                         "enable.auto.commit": False})
    consumer.assign([TopicPartition("payments-avro", 0, OFFSET_BEGINNING)])
    idle = 0
    while idle < 3:
        msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
        if msg is None:
            idle += 1
            continue
        if msg.error():
            continue
        schema_id, record = decode(msg.value(), reader)
        print(f"written with schema {schema_id}, read as {reader}: {record}")
    consumer.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Stream processing: tables, windows, joins and state
modules.summary: Processing streams on Kafka: the duality of streams and tables, event time, windows and grace periods, stream-table and stream-stream joins with their co-partitioning rule, fault-tolerant state, and the limits of exactly-once.

lessons.title: Streams and tables
objectives: Explain the duality of streams and tables
Choose between Kafka Streams, Flink and lighter-weight processors
key_points: A stream is an unbounded sequence of independent events, such as orders; a table holds the latest value for each key, such as each customer's current region, and every change to it is an event.
The two convert into each other: replaying a changelog stream builds a table, and recording every update to a table produces a changelog stream; a compacted topic is a table's durable changelog.

Kafka Streams, a Java library that runs inside your application, models these as KStream, KTable and GlobalKTable, which holds a full copy of a table in every instance; ksqlDB offers the same ideas in SQL.

Apache Flink and Spark Structured Streaming run jobs on their own clusters and read and write Kafka through connectors; Python libraries, or plain consumers and producers as in the lab, suit smaller jobs.

Stateless operations, such as filter and map, handle each record alone; stateful ones, such as counts, aggregations, windows and joins, must remember earlier records, and that state has to survive failures.

lessons.title: Time and windows in Kafka
objectives: Distinguish event time from processing time in Kafka records
Configure tumbling, hopping and session windows with a grace period
key_points: Every record has a timestamp: CreateTime, set by the producer and usually the event time, or LogAppendTime, set by the broker, chosen per topic with message.timestamp.type; producers can also set the timestamp explicitly.
Windows group records by event time: tumbling windows are fixed and don't overlap, hopping windows are fixed but overlap, and session windows grow with activity and close after a gap of inactivity.

Stream time is the highest timestamp a processor has seen; records can arrive out of order, so a window stays open until stream time passes its end plus a grace period, and later records for it are dropped as late.
Kafka Streams has asked for the grace period explicitly since version 3.0, as in TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace; a longer grace accepts more late data but delays final results and holds more state.

Windowed aggregations emit updated results as records arrive unless told otherwise; suppressing until the window closes emits one final result per window, which downstream systems such as alerting usually want.

lessons.title: Joins, state and the limits of exactly-once
objectives: Explain stream-table and stream-stream joins and co-partitioning
Describe how stream processors keep state fault-tolerant, and what exactly-once still leaves to you
key_points: A stream-table join enriches each event with the table's current value for its key, such as an order with its customer's region; it uses the value at processing time, so a later table update doesn't change results already emitted.
A stream-stream join matches events from two streams by key within a time window, such as a payment within 10 minutes of its order, because both sides are unbounded.

Joins need co-partitioning: both topics with the same number of partitions and the same key and partitioner; if not, the data must be repartitioned by key first, and Kafka Streams creates repartition topics for this, while GlobalKTable joins avoid it.

Kafka Streams keeps state in local stores, RocksDB by default, each backed by a compacted changelog topic; after a failure another instance restores the store from the changelog, and standby replicas make that quick.

exactly_once_v2 makes a Kafka Streams application's reads, state updates and writes atomic, but effects outside Kafka, such as calls to other services, still need idempotence, and reprocessing old data recomputes results unless you plan for it.

"""Send the customer table and a stream of timestamped orders for the windowing lab.

customers is a compacted topic: the latest value per key wins, and a null value (a tombstone) deletes the key.
Each order carries its event time as the record's timestamp, and some arrive out of order.
Usage:  python send_stream.py
"""
import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from confluent_kafka import Producer

BASE = datetime(2025, 3, 1, 12, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)

CUSTOMERS = [
    ("c-1", {"name": "Somchai", "region": "Central"}),
    ("c-2", {"name": "Nok", "region": "North"}),
    ("c-3", {"name": "Anan", "region": "North"}),
    ("c-3", {"name": "Anan", "region": "South"}),   # moved: the later value replaces the earlier one
    ("c-4", {"name": "Pim", "region": "East"}),
    ("c-4", None),                                  # tombstone: customer c-4 is deleted
    ("c-5", {"name": "Lek", "region": "Central"}),
]
ORDERS = [  # seconds after 12:00:00, customer, amount; listed in the order they arrive
    (5, "c-1", 120.0), (20, "c-2", 80.0), (50, "c-3", 200.0), (70, "c-1", 60.0), (55, "c-2", 40.0),
    (100, "c-4", 90.0), (58, "c-3", 70.0), (135, "c-5", 150.0), (155, "c-1", 30.0), (220, "c-2", 10.0),
]


def main():
    producer = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092", "enable.idempotence": True})
    for key, value in CUSTOMERS:
        producer.produce("customers", key=key, value=None if value is None else json.dumps(value))
    base_ms = int(BASE.timestamp() * 1000)
    for n, (seconds, customer, amount) in enumerate(ORDERS, 1):
        producer.produce("orders-stream", key=customer, timestamp=base_ms + seconds * 1000,
                         value=json.dumps({"order_id": 8000 + n, "customer": customer, "amount": amount}))
    producer.flush(10)
    print(f"Sent {len(CUSTOMERS)} customer records and {len(ORDERS)} orders")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Enrich orders with the customer's region (a stream-table join) and total revenue per region in
one-minute tumbling windows of event time, accepting events up to 30 seconds late.

Usage:  python windows.py
"""
import json
import uuid
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from confluent_kafka import OFFSET_BEGINNING, Consumer, Producer, TopicPartition

WINDOW_MS = 60_000
GRACE_MS = 30_000
BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"


def read_all(topic):
    """Read a topic from the beginning to its current end; return its records in order."""
    consumer = Consumer({"bootstrap.servers": BOOTSTRAP, "group.id": f"windows-{uuid.uuid4()}",
                         "enable.auto.commit": False})
    partitions = consumer.list_topics(topic, timeout=10).topics[topic].partitions
    consumer.assign([TopicPartition(topic, p, OFFSET_BEGINNING) for p in sorted(partitions)])
    records, idle = [], 0
    while idle < 3:
        msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
        if msg is None:
            idle += 1
        elif not msg.error():
            records.append(msg)
    consumer.close()
    return records


def load_table(records):
    """Build the table a compacted topic describes: latest value per key; a tombstone deletes the key."""
    table = {}
    for msg in records:
        key = msg.key().decode()
        # TODO 1: a record with a null value is a tombstone: remove the key from the table instead.
        table[key] = json.loads(msg.value())
    return table


def hhmm(ms, seconds=False):
    return datetime.fromtimestamp(ms / 1000, tz=timezone.utc).strftime("%H:%M:%S" if seconds else "%H:%M")


def main():
    customers = load_table(read_all("customers"))
    print("Customer table:", {k: v["region"] for k, v in sorted(customers.items())})
    producer = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": BOOTSTRAP})
    windows = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(float))   # window start -> region -> revenue
    stream_time = 0                                      # the highest event time seen so far

    def close_ready():
        for start in sorted(windows):
            if stream_time >= start + WINDOW_MS + GRACE_MS:
                totals = windows.pop(start)
                for region, revenue in sorted(totals.items()):
                    producer.produce("revenue-by-region", key=f"{hhmm(start)}|{region}",
                                     value=json.dumps({"window_start": hhmm(start), "region": region,
                                                       "revenue": round(revenue, 2)}))
                summary = ", ".join(f"{r} {v:.2f}" for r, v in sorted(totals.items()))
                print(f"Window {hhmm(start)}-{hhmm(start + WINDOW_MS)} closed: {summary}")

    for msg in read_all("orders-stream"):
        order = json.loads(msg.value())
        _, event_ms = msg.timestamp()
        start = event_ms - event_ms % WINDOW_MS
        # TODO 2: if this order's window has already closed (its start + WINDOW_MS + GRACE_MS is at or
        # before stream_time), print a "Late: order ... dropped" line and skip the order.
        region = customers.get(order["customer"], {}).get("region", "unknown")
        windows[start][region] += order["amount"]
        stream_time = max(stream_time, event_ms)
        close_ready()
    producer.flush(10)
    for start in sorted(windows):
        print(f"Window {hhmm(start)}-{hhmm(start + WINDOW_MS)} still open at stream time {hhmm(stream_time, seconds=True)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: msg.value() is None for a tombstone; table.pop(key, None) removes a key that may not be there.
A window starting at start closes when stream_time >= start + WINDOW_MS + GRACE_MS.
Delete and recreate the revenue-by-region topic if you want the console consumer to show only your latest run.

project.title: Build a real-time delivery monitor
project.brief: A food-delivery platform wants a live view of its city: orders per zone per minute, late deliveries, and riders who go quiet. Build the streaming pipeline on Kafka 4 in KRaft mode with Python (or Kafka Streams if you know Java). A simulator produces order and rider-location events with event timestamps, some out of order and some duplicated, keyed so each order's events stay in order. A validator checks every event against an Avro schema in the registry wire format and splits valid from rejected events in transactions, exactly once. A windowed processor joins orders with a compacted zone table and emits final per-zone counts for one-minute windows with a grace period, plus an alert when a delivery takes longer than its promised time. Show that the pipeline survives a consumer crash without double counting, that a compatible schema change ships without downtime, and that consumer lag stays under control.
deliverables: A topic design: each topic's key, partition count, retention or compaction, and why, with the commands or scripts that create them
The simulator, validator and windowed processor, with a README explaining how to run them against a local broker
The Avro schemas, with one compatible change (v2) and the compatibility test that proves it, deployed while the pipeline runs
Evidence of exactly-once validation: read_committed and read_uncommitted counts before and after a forced abort or crash
The windowed results and alerts for a fixed simulation run, with late events counted and explained
A failure test: kill the processor mid-run, restart it, and show the results match an uninterrupted run, or explain and bound any difference
A design note (one to two pages) on delivery semantics end to end, where state lives, how lag is monitored, and what you'd change for ten times the traffic

rubric.name: Topic and partition design
rubric.description: Keys preserve the ordering that matters, partition counts and retention or compaction are justified, and the zone table is a compacted topic.

rubric.name: Correct, reliable processing
rubric.description: Validation is transactional with read_committed downstream; duplicates in the input don't inflate results; the crash test passes or its difference is explained.

rubric.name: Windows, joins and late data
rubric.description: One-minute event-time windows with a grace period emit one final result each; late events are handled deliberately; the zone join is correct after table updates.

rubric.name: Schemas and evolution
rubric.description: Records carry a schema ID; the v2 change is tested for compatibility and deployed in the right upgrade order.

rubric.name: Operations
rubric.description: Consumer lag and errors are visible, for example from kafka-consumer-groups.sh or metrics, and the README lets someone else run the system.

rubric.name: Design note
rubric.description: A clear account of the guarantees at each step, including side effects outside Kafka, and realistic plans for scale.

project.submit: Paste your topic design, a link to your repository (or the code of each program), the outputs that show exactly-once validation, the windowed results, the crash test and the schema change, and your design note.
